2027-04-11.title: Third Sunday of Easter
readings: You killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead
Lord, let your face shine on us (or: Alleluia)
He is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world
Thus it is written, that the Messiah is to suffer and to rise from the dead on the third day
2027-04-11.alt: Year B. Third Sunday of Easter. Gloria and Creed; in Eastertide the Rite for the Blessing and Sprinkling of Water may replace the Penitential Act. The Regina Caeli is prayed at noon. St Stanislaus, bishop and martyr (11 Apr), is not celebrated this year because the Sunday prevails. Liturgical colour: white.
2027-04-11.verse: Look at my hands and my feet; see that it is I myself. Touch me and see; for a ghost does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.
theo: On the Third Sunday of Easter the Church sits us down in Jerusalem on the evening of the first Easter day. The two disciples have just run back from Emmaus and are telling “how he had been made known to them in the breaking of the bread.” Before St Luke shows us the risen Lord again, the first reading lets us hear what the apostles did with that experience. In Solomon's Portico, after the healing of the lame man, Peter speaks to the crowd: “The God of Abraham, the God of Isaac, and the God of Jacob, the God of our ancestors has glorified his servant Jesus.” He names the tragedy plainly: “you rejected the Holy and Righteous One and asked to have a murderer given to you, and you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. To this we are witnesses.” Then his tone changes completely: “And now, friends, I know that you acted in ignorance, as did also your rulers.” These are not words of condemnation but of a brother; they echo Jesus' own prayer from the cross, “Father, forgive them; for they do not know what they are doing.” Peter, who denied the Lord three times, is in no position to accuse anyone. The Church has always taught that the sins of all of us brought Christ to the cross and that the Jewish people may not be held collectively responsible for his death (Nostra Aetate 4; Catechism 597–598). Peter's purpose is the same as ours today: “Repent therefore, and turn to God so that your sins may be wiped out.” The Psalm is the prayer of one who has turned back: “Let the light of your face shine on us, O LORD!”

The second reading, from the First Letter of St John, is tender and strong. “My little children, I am writing these things to you so that you may not sin.” The Easter life is a life without sin, and John does not lower the standard. But he knows his children: “But if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous; and he is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and not for ours only but also for the sins of the whole world.” The Greek word for advocate is parakletos, the same word Jesus uses for the Holy Spirit. Jesus is our first advocate, standing before the Father with the wounds of his love; and the word for atoning sacrifice, hilasmos, recalls the mercy seat of the Ark, where the blood of atonement was sprinkled. He is not only the lawyer who pleads for us; he is himself the offering that reconciles. Then John gives a simple test for a living faith: “Now by this we may be sure that we know him, if we obey his commandments.” Knowing Christ is not a feeling but a life: “whoever obeys his word, truly in this person the love of God has reached perfection.”

Then the Gospel. “While they were talking about this, Jesus himself stood among them and said to them, ‘Peace be with you.’” They are “startled and terrified,” thinking they see a ghost. Jesus' answer is one of the most important texts in the Bible for our faith in the bodily Resurrection: “Look at my hands and my feet; see that it is I myself. Touch me and see; for a ghost does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have.” He shows them his wounds. And while “in their joy they were disbelieving and still wondering,” he asks a homely question: “Have you anything here to eat?” They give him a piece of broiled fish, “and he took it and ate in their presence.” The risen Christ is not a memory, not an idea, not a spirit only: he is the same Jesus, body and soul, now glorified, never to die again. Then he opens their minds to understand the Scriptures: “everything written about me in the law of Moses, the prophets, and the psalms must be fulfilled.” The whole Old Testament, all three parts, points to him. And he gives them their mission: “repentance and forgiveness of sins is to be proclaimed in his name to all nations, beginning from Jerusalem. You are witnesses of these things.” This Sunday has the same shape as every Mass: the Lord stands among us and says Peace; he opens the Scriptures; he gives himself as food; and he sends us out as witnesses.
conn: Greek archegos, the pioneer or founder who leads the way (Acts 3:15; Hebrews 12:2). The irony is deliberate: men put to death the very source of life, and God raised him.

Peter's words echo Jesus' prayer on the cross (Luke 23:34). The Church teaches that responsibility for the Passion may not be laid on all Jews then or now, and that all sinners are its authors (Catechism 597–598; Nostra Aetate 4).
Greek parakletos, one called to stand beside another, especially in court. In 1 John 2:1 it is Jesus; in John 14:16 Jesus promises “another Advocate,” the Holy Spirit (Catechism 692).
Greek hilasmos, linked with the mercy seat (hilasterion) over the Ark, where the high priest sprinkled blood on the Day of Atonement (Leviticus 16). Christ is both priest and victim.
The risen Jesus is not a ghost. His body is real, can be touched and can eat, yet is glorified, no longer bound by space and time (Catechism 645).
He eats not because he needs food but to show that he is truly alive and the same Jesus they knew. The fish (Greek ichthys) later became an early Christian symbol of Christ.
The law, the prophets and the psalms.
The three parts of the Jewish Scriptures (Torah, Prophets, Writings, of which the Psalms are the best known). Jesus says that all of it speaks of him (Luke 24:44).
The programme of the Acts of the Apostles: from Jerusalem to Judea and Samaria and to the ends of the earth (Acts 1:8). The word witnesses, martyres, would come to mean those who gave their blood.
altar: The Lord who said “Touch me and see” and ate the broiled fish gives us at this altar not a symbol but his own risen Body and Blood. We do not see his hands and feet, but we receive him truly, really and substantially present.
Jesus is the atoning sacrifice for our sins, and the Mass makes that one sacrifice present. Here our Advocate pleads for us, and from here we are sent as witnesses of repentance and forgiveness.
outline: Ask: if the risen Jesus stood in your house tonight, what would you want to touch, and what would you want to ask him?
Peter's preaching: tragedy named, mercy offered.
Point 3 · An advocate with the Father
Jesus our defender and our sacrifice.
The risen body, the opened Scriptures, the mission.
A table at night, a plate with a piece of fish, and a pair of wounded hands.
live: John says: if anyone does sin, we have an advocate. Make a good confession this Easter season and receive the peace of the risen Lord.
Each day this week read one Old Testament passage that points to Christ (for example Isaiah 53, Psalm 22, Psalm 16) and ask him to open your mind.
The risen Lord ate with his friends. Invite to your table this week someone who usually eats alone.
Speak of what you have seen
Tell one person this week, simply, how you have met the risen Lord in your life.
fathers: I know and believe that he was in the flesh even after the resurrection. When he came to Peter and those with him, he said to them: take hold of me, handle me, and see that I am not a bodiless spirit. And at once they touched him and believed.

John did not say, you have an advocate, but we have an advocate. He placed himself among the sinners, so that he might have Christ as his advocate. Let no one say: Peter is my advocate, or Paul; we have one Advocate, Christ.

The Lord ate after his resurrection not out of need but out of power. The earth absorbs water in one way, and the burning sun in another: the one from thirst, the other by its strength. So his risen body took food without any need.
magis: The appearances of the risen Christ; his real body, which can be touched and shares their meal, yet glorified.
“It is I myself”: Christ rose with his own body, and so shall we.
Responsibility for the death of Jesus is not to be laid on the Jews as a people; all sinners are its authors.
Jesus, the first Advocate, and the Holy Spirit, “another Advocate.”
Conversion and repentance, to which the risen Lord calls every Christian.
saints: St Stanislaus (11 Apr, not celebrated this year)
Bishop of Kraków, killed in 1079, according to tradition while celebrating Mass, after he had rebuked King Bolesław II. Patron of Poland; his memorial gives way to the Sunday this year.

12–17 Apr: Easter weekdays of the Third Week, with the Bread of Life chapter of John. 13 Apr: St Martin I, pope and martyr (optional). 18 Apr: Fourth Sunday of Easter, Good Shepherd Sunday, World Day of Prayer for Vocations.
2027-04-11.prayer: May your people exult for ever, O God, in renewed youthfulness of spirit, so that, rejoicing now in the restored glory of our adoption, we may look forward in confident hope to the rejoicing of the day of resurrection. Through our Lord Jesus Christ, your Son, who lives and reigns with you in the unity of the Holy Spirit, God, for ever and ever. Amen. Let us also pray: Risen Lord Jesus, you stood among your frightened disciples and said, Peace be with you. Show us your hands and your feet; open our minds to understand the Scriptures; feed us with your Body; and make us witnesses of repentance and forgiveness to all nations, beginning from our own homes. Alleluia. Amen.

quick: Peter told the crowd that God raised Jesus, the Author of life, and called them to repent so that their sins might be wiped out.
St John says: if anyone sins, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ, the atoning sacrifice for our sins.
The risen Jesus showed his hands and feet, ate a piece of fish, opened the Scriptures and made the disciples his witnesses.
2027-04-11.action: Invite someone who usually eats alone to share a meal with your family this week.
2027-04-11.question: Do I believe that Jesus rose in his real body, and does that belief change how I treat my own body and others?
catechism: The risen body of Jesus: real, touchable, yet glorified.
Conversion is the first call of the Gospel.
kidsaint: Stanislaus was a bishop in Poland long ago. The king was doing very bad things and hurting people, and Bishop Stanislaus bravely told him to stop. According to tradition, the king was so angry that he killed the bishop while he was saying Mass. Lesson: like the apostles, we must tell the truth about Jesus even when it is hard.
2027-04-11.special: Third Sunday of Easter (Year B). Gloria and Creed; sprinkling with water may replace the Penitential Act. Regina Caeli at noon.
term: The faith of the Church that Jesus rose from the dead in his own real body, the body that was crucified, now glorified and immortal; not a ghost and not merely a memory (Luke 24:39; Catechism 645). It is also the promise for us: we believe in the resurrection of the body.

family.explain: The disciples were talking together when suddenly Jesus was standing with them! They were scared and thought he was a ghost. Jesus said: look at my hands and feet; touch me! A ghost does not have a body like me. Then he asked for some food, and ate a piece of fish in front of them. Jesus is really alive!
family.intention: We pray for people who are afraid or who find it hard to believe.
family.ask: Ask: “Why did Jesus eat fish in front of his friends?” Then share a meal together and thank Jesus that he is alive.

illus: In a parish in Thrissur, a young engineer who had stopped believing told his grandmother that the Resurrection was only a beautiful story the disciples told to comfort themselves. She did not argue. She took out her old Bible, opened it to Luke 24 and asked him to read verse 39 aloud. Then she said: frightened men who think they have seen a ghost do not invent a story about touching wounds and watching him eat fish. And men who invent a comfort do not die for it. He went home and read the whole chapter. A year later he was a catechist.

pm.open: Risen Lord Jesus, stand among us now and say, Peace be with you. Open our minds to understand the Scriptures. Alleluia. Amen.
share: You killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead (Acts 3:15). How have my own sins taken part in the Passion, and how do I receive his forgiveness?
If anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father (1 John 2:1). Do I go to Jesus as my advocate after I sin, or do I hide?
Touch me and see (Luke 24:39). How do I touch the risen Lord today, in the sacraments and in the poor?
pm.resp: Lord, let your face shine on us.
interc: For the Church, that she may proclaim repentance and forgiveness to all nations.
For those who doubt the Resurrection, that the Lord may open their minds and hearts.
For friendship between Christians and the Jewish people, and for an end to all contempt.
For sinners who are afraid to come back, that they may know Jesus as their advocate.
For our group, that we may be witnesses of these things.
pm.close: Father, your Son showed his wounds and opened the Scriptures to his disciples. Make us faithful witnesses of his Resurrection. Through Christ our Lord. Amen.

homily: Dear brothers and sisters, the disciples are gathered in Jerusalem on the evening of Easter. The two from Emmaus are telling their story. And suddenly Jesus himself stands among them and says: Peace be with you. They are terrified. They think they are seeing a ghost.

Jesus does not scold them. He says: look at my hands and my feet; see that it is I myself. Touch me and see; for a ghost does not have flesh and bones as you see that I have (Luke 24:39). And then he asks: have you anything here to eat? He eats a piece of fish in front of them. Our faith is not in a ghost or a memory. Jesus rose in his real body, the same body that was crucified, now glorified for ever.

Why does this matter for us? Because our bodies matter. The body that works in the field, the body that is sick in the hospital, the body that grows old, is not thrown away. We believe in the resurrection of the body. And because the risen Lord has a body, he can give it to us. At this altar he gives us not a symbol but his own risen Body and Blood.

In the first reading Peter speaks to the crowd in Jerusalem: you killed the Author of life, whom God raised from the dead. But then he says: I know that you acted in ignorance. Repent, and turn to God so that your sins may be wiped out (Acts 3:17, 19). Peter had denied Jesus three times. He knows what forgiveness is. He does not preach blame; he preaches mercy. And the Church teaches that all of us, by our sins, share in the Passion.

St John says the same in the second reading: if anyone does sin, we have an advocate with the Father, Jesus Christ the righteous (1 John 2:1). When we fall, we are not alone before the Father. Jesus stands beside us, showing his wounds, pleading for us. That is why the sacrament of confession is an Easter sacrament: the risen Lord breathes peace on our sins.

Finally Jesus opens their minds to understand the Scriptures and says: you are witnesses of these things (Luke 24:48). We too have been with him today. We have heard his word, we will receive his Body. Let us go out as witnesses: with peace in our hearts, mercy on our lips, and a table open to those who eat alone. Alleluia. Amen.
kids: Children, when Jesus came to his friends after Easter, they thought he was a ghost! But Jesus said: touch my hands and my feet. Ghosts don't have bodies! And then he ate some fish in front of them. Yum! Jesus is really, really alive.
Today at Mass, Jesus comes to us in Holy Communion. We cannot see his hands, but he is really there. Let us say thank you, Jesus, because you are alive!

intro: Theme: “Touch me and see; you are witnesses of these things.”
The Author of life raised, repentance offered, our Advocate with the Father, and the risen body that sends us out.

sub: The God of Abraham glorifies his servant.

points.apply: Spend five minutes before a crucifix this week and let the Lord show you how your sins are part of the story he has forgiven.

The atoning sacrifice for the whole world.

Jesus is our Advocate and our sacrifice; he rose in his real body, opens the Scriptures and sends us as witnesses.
